title: Minimum Changes to Make K Semi-palindromes
statement:
Cut the string `s` into exactly `k` non-empty contiguous pieces, then edit letters so that every piece is a **semi-palindrome**. One edit replaces a single character with any lowercase letter. Return the fewest edits needed over all ways of cutting.

A string `t` of length `L` is a semi-palindrome when some `d` with `1 <= d < L` divides `L` such that, for every offset `r` from `0` to `d - 1`, the characters `t[r], t[r + d], t[r + 2d], ...` read the same forwards and backwards. With `d = 1` this is an ordinary palindrome. A string of length 1 has no such `d`, so it is never a semi-palindrome; every piece must therefore have length at least 2.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every way to cut `s` into `k` pieces is exponential, but the pieces are independent: the cheapest total is the cheapest way to cut a prefix into `k - 1` pieces plus the cost of the last piece. So precompute `cost[start][end]`, the fewest edits that turn `s[start..end)` into a semi-palindrome, then run a DP over (number of pieces, prefix length). For one piece and one divisor `d`, each group `r, r + d, ...` must become a palindrome, which takes one edit per mismatched pair; two pointers walking inwards from both ends of the group count those pairs.

## Approach

1. For every substring `s[start..end)` of length `len >= 2` and every divisor `d < len` of `len`, count `changes`: for each offset `r`, put `left` at `start + r` and `right` at `end - d + r`, step them towards each other by `d`, and count the pairs that differ.
2. Keep the smallest count over all `d` in `cost[start][end]`.
3. Let `dp[parts][end]` be the fewest edits for cutting `s[0..end)` into `parts` pieces; `dp[0][0] = 0`.
4. For each `parts` and `end`, try every `start` of the last piece (leaving room for 2 letters per piece): `dp[parts - 1][start] + cost[start][end]`.
5. Return `dp[k][n]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "abcac"`, `k = 2`. Some costs: `cost[0][2] = 1` (`"ab"` needs one edit), `cost[2][5] = 0` (`"cac"` is a palindrome), `cost[0][3] = 1` (`"abc"`), `cost[3][5] = 1` (`"ac"`). The two-piece cuts give `"ab" + "cac" = 1 + 0` and `"abc" + "ac" = 1 + 1`, so `dp[2][5] = 1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n³ · D + k · n²), where D is the number of divisors of a length (at most 17 here): each substring and divisor costs O(len), and each DP cell tries O(n) starts.
- Space: O(n² + k · n) for `cost` and `dp`.

## Pitfalls

- A piece of length 1 is never a semi-palindrome; never let a piece be shorter than 2.
- `d` must be a proper divisor: `d = len` would make every string trivially valid.
- Take the minimum over all divisors; a string may be cheap for `d = 2` and expensive for `d = 1`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cost[start][end]` | fewest edits to make `s[start..end)` a semi-palindrome |
| `len`, `d` | piece length and the divisor being tried |
| `r`, `left`, `right` | group offset and the two pointers inside that group |
| `changes` | mismatched pairs for this piece and `d` |
| `dp[parts][end]` | fewest edits to cut `s[0..end)` into `parts` pieces |
